evaluation.positioning_hook: A panic-prone homicide sergeant is recruited into a secret anti-terror program, then discovers the enemy he’s hunting is his own violent double.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean commercial engine: a cop thriller that escalates into sci-fi action, with a hero whose panic disorder becomes the key to survival. The audience promise is immediate, though the script’s extreme pulp violence and very specific mythology narrow it below broad four-quadrant play.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early and hard: Jack Madison investigates a string of bizarre killings, gets folded into Ramsey’s classified operation, and learns the threat is a split-off negative self. The opening car-lot massacre, the cult imagery, and the later reveal all point to the same engine with very little ambiguity.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Madison is a workable lead because he’s competent, funny, anxious, and morally grounded, especially in the child-support and Brandy scenes. Ramsey is a strong foil with enough mystery to carry the movie, but several supporting characters function more as vivid genre pieces than deeply durable people.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits to a wild mash-up of police procedural, body-horror, and militarized sci-fi without apologizing for it. The split-self mythology, plasma weapons, and cult-terror framework give it a distinct lane rather than a generic action template.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: It moves with real forward drive once the case begins to connect to Rabinski, the Dominion, and then Roger. The back half is especially propulsive, though the early procedural stretch and repeated explanatory passages slow the momentum before the big reveal.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea feels both strange and legible: a man literally fighting the worst version of himself while a secret government unit hunts human-seeming monsters. That combination of psychological metaphor and genre mechanics is memorable and commercially sticky.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The world has its own rules, hierarchy, and tech — Gov-Ops, Separatists, enzyme weapons, the testing program, the hidden garage lab. It’s story-generating, though the mythology is delivered more through exposition than through lived-in institutional texture.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a very specific B-movie swagger: hardboiled banter, grotesque violence, and deadpan one-liners sitting beside earnest emotional beats. That tonal confidence is one of its biggest assets and makes the material feel authored.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are real thematic seeds here — identity, aggression, masculinity, duty, and the cost of repression — but the script mostly surfaces them through plot mechanics and speeches. The material suggests more depth than it fully cashes in on.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Madison/Ramsey is the engine, and Kat adds a second strong axis, but the script is still fundamentally lead-driven. The supporting players are memorable, yet most relationships are functional rather than generative enough to create a dense ensemble system.

lead_characters.name: Jack Madison
lead_characters.demographics: Black man, late 30s, NYPD homicide sergeant, father, divorced, anxiety disorder.
lead_characters.hook: A hard-working homicide sergeant who talks like a streetwise pro but lives with panic attacks he’s learned to hide. He’s honorable, dryly funny, and physically capable, yet the real fight is internal: he has to keep functioning while his own violent double is literally hunting him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Denzel Washington in Training Day or Michael B. Jordan in Creed — a role that lets an actor play authority, vulnerability, humor, and physical command in the same frame. The panic attacks, the deadpan one-liners, and the final self-confrontation give the performer a full-range star turn.

lead_characters.name: William Ramsey
lead_characters.demographics: White man, late 40s, FBI/Army covert operative, physically fit, classified government background.
lead_characters.hook: A polished, sly federal operator who reads as a smug consultant until the movie reveals he’s been carrying the secret architecture of the whole war. He’s part mentor, part manipulator, part action-movie wizard, and the script keeps him just opaque enough to stay dangerous.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Tommy Lee Jones in The Fugitive or J.K. Simmons in Whiplash a chance to dominate scenes with precision and authority. The appeal is the controlled charisma: a man who can explain the impossible, crack a joke, and still feel like he’s hiding a second movie underneath.

lead_characters.name: Katherine Lopez
lead_characters.demographics: Latina woman, 30s-40s, military veteran, covert arms broker, mother.
lead_characters.hook: A lethal, hyper-competent operator who can seduce, negotiate, and kill in the same breath. Her toughness is complicated by the loss of her daughter, which gives her a real emotional bruise under the swagger and makes her more than just the movie’s femme fatale.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of part that gave Charlize Theron in Atomic Blonde or Michelle Rodriguez in Girlfight a chance to be both physically dominant and emotionally guarded. The role offers a rare mix of sex appeal, command, and grief-driven ferocity.

lead_characters.name: Roger
lead_characters.demographics: Male, ageless/unclear, leader of the Dominion/Separatists, physically superhuman.
lead_characters.hook: The hidden architect of the movement, introduced as a myth and paid off as the literal violent self that has been steering the chaos. He’s not just a villain; he’s the embodiment of appetite, aggression, and domination given a face.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of villain role that gave Heath Ledger in The Dark Knight or Javier Bardem in No Country for Old Men a chance to become the movie’s gravitational force. The part is built for an actor who can make menace feel intelligent, seductive, and deeply personal.

lead_characters.name: Brandy
lead_characters.demographics: Black woman, 20s-30s, Madison’s girlfriend, mother of Tommy.
lead_characters.hook: A volatile, sexual, combative presence whose scenes keep shifting from domestic friction to outright supernatural threat. She’s written as both a relationship complication and a horror beat, which makes her memorable even when the movie is using her as a pressure point.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Regina Hall in Support the Girls or Taraji P. Henson in No Good Deed a chance to pivot between charm, danger, and volatility. The part asks for a performer who can turn a domestic scene into a genre event.

lead_characters.name: Tommy
lead_characters.demographics: Boy, about 7 years old, Brandy’s son.
lead_characters.hook: At first he reads as a sweet kid in the apartment, then the movie reveals the terrifying split between the child and the monster inside him. He’s a small role with a huge genre function: the moment the script makes the supernatural rules feel personal and invasive.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of eerie child role that made Haley Joel Osment in The Sixth Sense unforgettable — a part where innocence and dread coexist in the same face. It’s a brief but high-impact showcase if cast right.

lead_characters.name: Kat Lopez
lead_characters.demographics: Latina woman, 30s-40s, arms dealer, military veteran, mother.
lead_characters.hook: A swaggering black-market power player who can run a weapons deal in heels and still feel emotionally wounded when her daughter is used against her. She’s one of the script’s best contradictions: sexually confident, militarily capable, and privately devastated.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Gina Gershon in Bound or Zoe Saldaña in Colombiana a chance to own the frame with attitude and physicality. The daughter reveal gives the actor a grief note that keeps the character from being pure style.

lead_characters.name: Frank Donnely
lead_characters.hook: A practical precinct boss who functions as the institutional bridge between Madison, Prosky, and Ramsey. He’s not flashy, but he helps sell the procedural world and gives the script a believable chain of command.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is solid character-actor territory in the vein of Albert Brooks in Drive or John Turturro in many cop-world supporting turns — a role that rewards authority, irritation, and dry timing.

casting_characteristics: villain and doubles require strong physical presence
multiple supporting roles can be cast with character actors

technical.vfx_details: Multiple split-self effects, body transformations, disintegration/ash effects, plasma weapon impacts, and the missile blast sequence require compositing and practical enhancement.
technical.sfx_needs: Gunfire, explosions, vehicle impacts, fire, electrocution effects, body-horror prosthetics, and practical blood/char effects.

rights_flags.detail: Glen Campbell's 'Gentle on My Mind' is specifically named and used in a plot-adjacent driving sequence.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release; best positioned as an R-rated genre title with action and sci-fi elements.

budget.note: Contemporary locations keep the base spend contained, but the freeway chase, warehouse/pier battle, missile blast, and repeated split-self effects will push this above a simple indie actioner.

casting.note: Jack Madison needs a lead who can carry action, comedy, and panic disorder without losing authority, while Ramsey and Kat both need actors with strong physical and tonal command.

development.note: The mythology is clear enough to follow, but the script leans on exposition for the bio-genetic backstory and Dominion rules, which is the main buyer conversation around clarity.

comp_set.title: The Hidden
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the buddy-cop structure, body-hopping menace, and hard-R genre energy of a cop thriller that turns into a sci-fi creature hunt.

comp_set.title: Split Second
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the pulpy, urban, high-concept action lane where a detective faces a monstrous threat in a grimy city setting.

comp_set.title: The Matrix
comp_set.why_it_comps: Not on budget, but on the idea of hidden reality, specialized weapons, and a protagonist learning the rules of a secret war.

comp_set.title: Upgrade
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the body-control, violent-double, and revenge-through-technology DNA in a lean genre package.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adult genre fans who like hard-R action with a sci-fi twist and a lead who can carry both jokes and violence.
audience_target.demographics: 18-49 skew, male-leaning but accessible to women through the relationship and character material; strongest with viewers who like elevated pulp and practical-action spectacle.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary settings and a limited cast help, but the freeway action, warehouse battle, missile sequence, and VFX body-splitting effects keep this above micro.

types_of_buyers: producer groups looking for a star-driven contained action swing
directors with practical-effects or comic-book-adjacent sensibilities
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where a buyer wants a clear hook, a male star vehicle, and enough spectacle to justify a theatrical or premium-streaming launch. The script’s mix of cop procedural, body horror, and secret-war mythology gives it a recognizable commercial shape without feeling generic.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature: the core engine resolves around Madison versus Roger and the negative-self mythology closes the loop. There isn’t a clean spinoff vector with a supporting character deep enough to anchor a separate franchise.

strengths.what_it_means: A buyer can pitch this in one sentence, which is a real advantage in a crowded genre market. That kind of clarity helps both development and marketing because the premise sells before the mythology has to do any work.
strengths.evidence: The opening car-lot massacre, Ramsey’s classified explanation, and the eventual reveal that Madison is fighting his own negative self all point to one clean engine.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Madison is a playable star role.
strengths.what_it_means: The lead combines authority, humor, vulnerability, and action competence, which is exactly what makes a mid-budget genre movie attachable. That gives the project a real shot at a recognizable actor who wants a showcase rather than a franchise obligation.
strengths.evidence: His dry one-liners at the crime scenes, the child-support material, and the panic-attack freeway sequence all define him as more than a generic cop.

strengths.what_it_means: The script knows how to be grotesque, funny, and earnest in the same breath, which makes it feel authored rather than assembled. Buyers looking for an elevated pulp lane will recognize that voice immediately.
strengths.evidence: The “Job security” line, Ramsey’s deadpan explanations, and the absurdly specific violence around the cult and body-splitting all carry the same swagger.

strengths.what_it_means: The movie keeps finding new ways to stage conflict — plasma rifles, freeway combat, a missile truck, and a final mass-incineration payoff. That gives the project trailer moments and a clear sense of escalation.
strengths.evidence: The synagogue standoff, the pier battle, the motorboat escape, and the Mills Creek rally sequence all build bigger than the last.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Kat and Ramsey widen the commercial lane.
strengths.what_it_means: The script isn’t just a solo male vehicle; it has two vivid supporting roles that can attract talent and broaden the appeal. That helps the package feel less like a one-note action piece and more like a world with multiple star turns.
strengths.evidence: Kat’s arms-dealer sequence and Ramsey’s reveal as the hidden operative both give the movie additional casting and marketing hooks.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, high-concept genre buy: a cop-thriller premise that mutates into body-horror sci-fi, anchored by a lead role with real star-play and a tone that knows exactly how pulpy it wants to be. The contemporary setting keeps the economics in a buyer-friendly lane while the action set pieces and split-self mythology give the package enough spectacle to feel eventful without needing tentpole money.

items.area: The mythology is front-loaded in exposition.
items.detail: Ramsey’s bio-genetic explanation, the Dominion/Separatist rules, and the negative-self mechanics are all delivered in dialogue-heavy bursts. That makes the concept clear, but it also means the movie asks the audience to process a lot of rule-setting before the emotional stakes fully lock in.

The script leans hard into dismemberment, immolation, body splitting, and cult slaughter, which is part of the appeal but also narrows the buyer pool. This is not a broad four-quadrant action title; it lives in the harder-R, genre-forward lane.

items.area: The lead depends on a very specific performance blend.
items.detail: Madison has to play cop authority, panic disorder, dry comedy, and physical action without tipping into parody or melodrama. That’s a strong showcase, but it narrows casting more than the page might suggest.

items.area: The named music cue needs a clearance pass.
items.detail: Glen Campbell’s 'Gentle on My Mind' is specifically named and used in the truck sequence, so that’s a real sync item if the scene stays intact. It’s not a deal-breaker, but it is a line item that has to be planned for.

issues.headline: The script’s biggest friction is not the premise — it’s the amount of rule explanation required to get the premise across, especially before the audience has fully bonded with Madison. The other buyer conversation is tonal: this is a hard-R, effects-driven genre swing with a very specific performance ask, which is a strength creatively but a narrower commercial lane.
